paragraphs: §1 — Daniel al-Qūmisī's "twenty years," and the divergence of the Rabbanites and ʿĀnān

It has been related of Daniel [al-Qūmisī] also that he used to hold that the obligations (al-farāʾiḍ) become binding only upon one who has reached twenty years of age, and that he based this upon the account of אנוש המדבר ("the men of the wilderness"), and [upon the fact] that Scripture did not impose the penalty upon those who refused to enter the Land except upon one who was twenty years old and upward [Num 14:29]. But I do not know whether this report concerning him is sound or not — except that a number of our Baṣran colleagues (aṣḥābunā al-Baṣriyyīn) have related, on the authority of some of their elders (mashāyikh), that he used to hold this view and to be convinced of it. As for the Rabbanites (al-Rabbāniyyīn), they imposed the commandments upon the thirteen-year-old (ibn thalāthata ʿashar sana) without any proof; and as for ʿĀnān, he did not impose [the law of] impurity (al-ṭamaʾ) except upon the five-year-old, and did not impose some of [the other obligations] except upon the twenty-year-old — and we shall mention that in its place.

: Anūsh al-mudabbar / אנוש המדבר is the OCR's reading (the Kraken witness had anshei ha-midbar, "the men of the wilderness"); both point to the wilderness generation of the spies (Num 14), whom Scripture condemned to die in the desert "from twenty years old and upward" (Num 14:29), excluding the under-twenties from the decree. This census-age of liability (cf. Num 1:3, the muster "from twenty years old"; and Exod 30:14, the half-shekel "from twenty years old") is the scriptural peg for al-Qūmisī's twenty-year threshold. : The bab opens by cataloguing three rival thresholds for legal majority: (a) Daniel al-Qūmisī — twenty, grounded in the spies' census-age; (b) the Rabbanites — thirteen (bar mitzvah, the Mishnaic ben shelosh-ʿesreh la-mitzvot, m. Avot 5:21), which Q dismisses as having "no proof"; and (c) ʿĀnān ben David — a graduated scheme (five for the laws of ritual impurity, twenty for some others). Q's hedge — that he cannot vouch for the report about al-Qūmisī, having it only at second hand through the Baṣran Karaites' transmission from their teachers — is characteristic of his scholarly caution; the same al-Qūmisī polemic was joined in Bab 21 (the defense of al-naẓar against al-Qūmisī) and Bab 22 (the angels). The deferred treatment ("in its place") of ʿĀnān's scheme points forward to Q's legal books (Maqalat V onward).
§2 — The twenty-year rule is contrary to reason: obligation tracks comprehension, not a fixed age

As for the view that the obligation becomes binding only upon the twenty-year-old — it is contrary to reason (bi-ḍidd al-ʿaql), since in it there is the permitting of killing, fornication, the profanation of the Sabbath, theft, and all the grave sins (al-kabāʾir) to whoever is nineteen years old. What is admissible in our view on this matter is rather that children are not equal in mind, intelligence, and quickness in learning — for we observe among children one who is five or six years old yet of excellent native wit and strong mind, who takes in what is set before him and retains it within a brief span; and another who is ten or twelve years old yet falls far short of that, and does not grasp it save after a long span. So we say: since the matter is so, then the binding force of the obligation varies among people according to the variation of their intelligence and their attainment in knowledge. Every obligation, then, becomes binding upon a person at his apprehending it and his coming to know it — in whatever time that may be, and at whatever age — and there is no fixed time for that, nor does it become binding [only] upon one of a particular age. The proof of that also is that there is no dispute that one who knew the obligation of the Sabbath before he knew the prohibition of eating swine's flesh — the bindingness of the Sabbath was upon him before the bindingness of the prohibition of eating swine's flesh; and likewise in all the obligations.

: Q's positive doctrine and the heart of the bab: legal obligation is a function of individual cognition, not of a calendar age. The reductio against the twenty-year rule is sharp — it would license the gravest crimes (murder, fornication, Sabbath-desecration, theft) to a nineteen-year-old. The empirical premise (children differ widely in intellectual maturity, a precocious six-year-old outpacing a dull twelve-year-old) grounds the conclusion that obligation attaches severally, commandment by commandment, the moment the individual comprehends each one. The closing argument — that one comes under the Sabbath obligation as soon as one knows it, even before knowing the swine-flesh prohibition — makes obligation per-commandment and per-person, exactly mirroring the naẓar/maʿrifa epistemology (obligation follows cognition) Q defends throughout Maqala III and against al-Qūmisī in Bab 21.
§3 — Binyamin al-Nahāwandī: instruction from weaning; and the scriptural proof that the call is to those who comprehend

And Binyamin [al-Nahāwandī] said that the instruction (taʿlīm) of the child becomes obligatory from the time he is weaned from milk, and he adduced as proof His saying [Isa 28:9] אֶת מִי יוֹרֶה דֵעָה וְאֶת מִי יָבִין שְׁמוּעָה ("whom shall He teach knowledge, and whom shall He make to understand the message?"), and he said [Isa 28:9] גְּמוּלֵי מֵחָלָב עַתִּיקֵי מִשָּׁדָיִם ("those weaned from milk, those drawn from the breasts"). And he confirmed that by the account of שמואל (Samuel), and [by what] Scripture said [1 Sam 1:24] ותעלהו עמה כאשר גמלתו ("and she brought him up with her when she had weaned him"). And he alleged that the weaning takes place at three years, on account of his saying [2 Chr 31:16] מלבד התיחשם לזכרים מבן שלש שנים ולמעלה כל הבא לבית יי ("apart from the reckoning of the males from three years old and upward, all who enter the house of the Lord") etc. So everything the child is taught from the time he reaches three years of age becomes obligatory for him to perform, at whatever time it may be. And this which we have said reason makes obligatory, and there is for it in Scripture a proof that makes it obligatory from the side of the report (min jihat al-khabar) — namely that we found it in עזרא (Ezra), following upon the prayer that is [Neh 9], that he says [Neh 9:38] ובכל זאת אנחנו כרתים אמנה ("and because of all this we are making a firm covenant") etc. ועל החתומים נחמיה ("and upon the sealed document [were] Nehemiah") etc.; and he says after that [Neh 10:15] ראשי העם פרעש ("the heads of the people: Parosh") etc.; and at the end of his mention of the people he says [Neh 10:29] ושאר העם הכהנים הלוים השוערים המשוררים הנתינים וכל הנבדל מעמי הארצות אל תורת האלהים נשיהם בניהם ובנותיהם כל יודע מבין ("and the rest of the people, the priests, the Levites, the gatekeepers, the singers, the temple-servants, and all who had separated themselves from the peoples of the lands to the Torah of God, their wives, their sons, and their daughters, everyone who had knowledge and understanding"). So he reported that they would summon to the book of God and His Torah only the one who was knowing and understanding (ʿāliman fahiman), to the exclusion of any other. And he says also in another place [Neh 8:2] וכל מבין לשמע ("and all who could understand what they heard"), and he says [Neh 10:29] ולהשבע אל דברי התורה ("and to take an oath to the words of the Torah"). So he stated explicitly, in both places together, that the calling and the reciting [of Scripture] is and becomes binding for the one who is understanding (fahman), to the exclusion of one who does not understand.

: The OCR carries a query-mark (`دليلٌ (?)`) over the word "proof" here; the reading is secure from context — Q is contrasting the rational warrant ("reason makes it obligatory") just given with a scriptural-evidentiary warrant ("from the side of the report") now to be adduced from Ezra–Nehemiah. : Q reports Binyamin al-Nahāwandī's competing benchmark — instruction begins at weaning (which Binyamin sets at three years, via 2 Chr 31:16's "from three years old"), supported by Isa 28:9 ("those weaned from milk") and the Samuel narrative (1 Sam 1:24). Q does not so much refute Binyamin as absorb him into his own comprehension-based doctrine: whatever the child is taught from age three binds him when he understands it. The Ezra–Nehemiah proof is the bab's positive scriptural anchor: the covenant-renewal assembly summons specifically "everyone who had knowledge and understanding" (kol yodeaʿ mevin, Neh 10:29; kol mevin li-shmoaʿ, Neh 8:2) — so the address of the Torah is, by Scripture's own account, to those capable of comprehending it, exactly as Q's reason-argument concluded. The verse-references in the source are heavily garbled in the OCR (the diff-report shows ~40 disagreements on this page alone) and have been normalized to the standard Masoretic loci.
§4 — Two adversaries deferred to earlier refutations: the rejecters of public proclamation, and the claimants that the promised temple is already built

As for what we have related of a people that they reject the public proclamation (al-jahr) and the report (al-khabar) — the refutation of them has already preceded, in the refutation of Ismāʿīl al-ʿUkbarī, with that which is sufficient against them. And likewise the statement of whoever alleged that the house promised to be built [Ezek 40–48] has [already] been completed — the refutation of them has [already] entered into the refutation of the Christians; save that we wish to mention here a portion of what is in Scripture, besides what we mentioned there, that refutes their statement and discredits it, and from which is made plain the calumny (baht) of whoever held this view and his obstinacy — [that being] in the bab that follows this bab, which is

: The bab closes by handing off two adjacent controversies to refutations already given (or about to be given). (a) The rejecters of al-jahr (public proclamation/recitation) and al-khabar (transmitted report) were dealt with "in the refutation of Ismāʿīl al-ʿUkbarī" — Ismāʿīl al-ʿUkbarī being an early-9th-c. sectary whom Q treats among the heterodox in Maqala I and answers earlier in the polemical sequence. (b) The claim that Ezekiel's promised temple (Ezek 40–48) has already been realized in the Second Temple was the very thesis Q demolished against the Christians in Bab 6 §§14–18 (the uncircumcised hold Jerusalem; the scale and permanence of Ezekiel's temple; the future-temple festivals and dietary laws) — and which he announces he will now press against the Jewish sectarians who share it in the following Bab 24. The sentence runs directly into the Bab 24 heading without a break; the transition word هو ("which is") governs the heading itself, so the bab ends on the title of its successor.

- The bab's subject. The heading — fī al-qawl ʿalā man kam tajib al-farāʾiḍ — concerns the age of legal majority: at what point, and upon whom, the commandments become binding. It is a short, self-contained halakhic-theoretical bab embedded in the run of intra-sectarian polemics (Babs 21–24) that target Daniel al-Qūmisī and his circle. Q surveys three rival fixed-age thresholds (al-Qūmisī's twenty, the Rabbanites' thirteen, ʿĀnān's graduated five/twenty) plus Binyamin al-Nahāwandī's weaning-at-three, and rejects every fixed threshold in favor of a cognitive criterion.

- Obligation as a function of cognition. Q's controlling thesis (§2) is that obligation attaches to the individual commandment by commandment as soon as the individual comprehends that commandment — not at any uniform age. This is the direct legal application of the naẓar/maʿrifa epistemology Q deploys throughout the Anwār: just as the rational obligation to know God arises with the maturation of the intellect, so each revealed obligation binds at the moment of its apprehension. The per-commandment corollary (one is bound by the Sabbath before the swine-flesh prohibition if one learned it first) is a striking and distinctively Qirqisānian sharpening.

- The reductio against fixed ages. The argument that a twenty-year threshold would license a nineteen-year-old to murder, fornicate, profane the Sabbath, steal, and commit "all the grave sins" (al-kabāʾir) is the bab's rhetorical centerpiece. It exposes the absurdity of any purely chronological criterion for all obligations at once, and motivates the move to a comprehension-indexed, commandment-by-commandment account.

- Binyamin absorbed, not refuted. Q treats Binyamin al-Nahāwandī's weaning-at-three benchmark not as a rival to be demolished but as data folded into his own view: instruction may begin at weaning, but obligation binds only with comprehension. The Ezra–Nehemiah covenant-assembly (Neh 8–10), summoning "everyone who had knowledge and understanding," is Q's scriptural clincher that revealed obligation is addressed to the comprehending.

- The closing hand-offs (§4). The bab ends by deferring two adjacent positions to refutations elsewhere: the rejecters of al-jahr and al-khabar (to "the refutation of Ismāʿīl al-ʿUkbarī") and the "temple already rebuilt" thesis (to the anti-Christian Bab 6, and now forward to Bab 24). The closing clause is grammatically continuous with the Bab 24 title, so the bab terminates on the heading of its successor — a clean confirmation of the boundary.

- OCR state. The Hebrew citations on p167 (§3) are badly corrupted in the Kraken witness; the multimodal re-OCR (preferred in the merged text) recovers most of them, and the verse-references — which Q writes in his usual heavily-abbreviated marginal-pointer style (כדשנ׳, בשם, etc.) — have been normalized to standard Masoretic loci against the diff-report. No textual lacuna; the bab is complete from heading to heading. The one query-marked word (the "proof" of §3, `دليلٌ (?)`) is secure from context.

Avot 5:21; b. Nazir 29b and b. Niddah 45b on the onset of obligation with the signs of puberty. - For Ismāʿīl al-ʿUkbarī and the al-jahr / al-khabar controversy deferred in §4: Q's own Maqala I doxography (the ʿUkbarites); cross-reference within the Anwār to the now-lost or earlier-placed "refutation of Ismāʿīl al-ʿUkbarī." - For the "temple already rebuilt" thesis** taken up against the sectarians in Bab 24: Bab 6 §§14–18 of this Maqala (the anti-Christian treatment of Ezekiel's future temple, Isa 52:1, Ezra 5:16, Jer 31:40, Zech 14:16–18).
